extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers interested in Kant and theories of taste/humour)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles about beauty, taste, and humour from a section of Kant's Critique of Judgement; concerned with what makes art, poetry, music, jokes, and 'humour' valuable or effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as purposive in beautiful art
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential thing in all beautiful art is the form, which is purposive as regards our observation and judgement; the pleasure is at the same time cultivation and disposes the spirit to Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with matter of sensation (charm or emotion): mere sensation yields enjoyment only, leaves nothing in the Idea, makes the spirit dull and the object distasteful; beautiful art's form should promote cultivation and further susceptibility to aesthetic Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with moral Ideas for self-sufficing satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the beautiful arts are not combined with moral Ideas, which alone bring self-sufficing satisfaction, they become merely a distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arts lacking connection to moral Ideas merely disperse discontent and risk making us more useless and dissatisfied; by contrast, when linked to moral Ideas they provide a lasting, self-contained satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's primacy: expansion of imagination and honest play of illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ranks highest among the arts: it expands the mind by setting the imagination at liberty and offers a wealth of thought rising aesthetically to Ideas; it plays with illusion but without deceiving, declaring itself mere play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is rooted in genius and resists precept or example; it strengthens the faculty that judges nature as phenomenon and serves as a schema for the supersensible. Its honesty (declaring itself play) prevents ensnaring the Understanding by sensory presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric (persuasive art) versus eloquence: avoid deceptive persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric insofar as it is the art of persuasion (ars oratoria) is a dialectic that borrows from poetry to win minds before judgement is formed, and thus is deceptive; it cannot be recommended for law courts or the pulpit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive art that seeks to captivate rather than inform is objectionable for matters requiring accurate knowledge or moral duty. Eloquence and style (mere elegance of speech) differ from manipulative rhetoric and are more acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music (art of tone) as transitory pleasure, not cultural formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Music moves the mind more intensely but only transitorily; it is primarily enjoyment rather than culture and ranks lower for the 'judgement of Reason' in terms of formative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music communicates universally via tone as a 'language of the affections' and rests on mathematical relations of vibration, which permits a universal claim for Taste; but it desires constant change, does not bear frequent repetition, and its impressions are typically transitory rather than permanent cultural products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's obtrusiveness compared to visual arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Music can extend its influence further than desired (diffuse widely) and thus obtrude on others, whereas visual arts allow avoidance by looking away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant compares music's diffusion to a smell: it forces itself on others and can 'do violence to the freedom of others,' an aesthetic drawback not present in sight-based arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative arts (e.g., painting) produce permanent cultural value
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative arts, which proceed from determinate Ideas to sensations, provide permanent products that serve as vehicles for concepts and thus supply greater cultural 'education' of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painting is given special praise among formative arts for penetrating further into the region of Ideas and extending the field of intuition in conformity with them; formative arts create lasting impressions that can be recalled and used for reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between satisfaction (aesthetic) and gratification (bodily pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference between what satisfies in the act of judging (aesthetic satisfaction) and what gratifies (pleasure in sensation), the latter being tied to bodily well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gratification often promotes a feeling of health and can be misleading when conflated with aesthetic satisfaction (examples: Epicurus, joy at inheritance despite poverty; sorrow of widow satisfying). Reason (approbation/disapprobation) governs satisfaction/dissatisfaction at a higher level than mere gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of free play of sensations: games, music, and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The free play of sensations (without a design) subdivides into play of fortune (games of chance), play of tone (music), and play of thought (wit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games require an interest (vanity or selfishness), music requires merely change of sensations tied to affections, and wit springs from changing representations without producing interest; wit and music animate the body via ideas but do not produce lasting cognitive gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of laughter: sudden transformation of strained expectation into nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is 'an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful jest contains something capable of deceiving for a moment; when the illusion is dissipated, the mind repeatedly checks it, producing rapid alternation of tension and relaxation and a bodily oscillation (e.g., the Indian/ale anecdote; the heir whose wig 'turned gray'). If an expected object simply proves false without that momentary deception, it displeases rather than amuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for comic effect: momentary deception/illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: For lively convulsive laughter there must be something absurd in which the Understanding can find no satisfaction; the jest must temporarily deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic depends on a brief illusion that is suddenly removed, producing a pleasurable bodily effect tied to restored equilibrium; mere exposure of a liar without that illusory set-up often fails to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naiveté as a rare humorous/esthetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Naiveté is the breaking-out of original sincerity in opposition to the art of dissimulation; it makes us laugh at simplicity that cannot dissemble while also blending seriousness and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation of naiveté in a fictitious person is possible and can be beautiful, though rare. Naiveté differs from open-hearted simplicity (which simply lacks social craft) and typically elicits both humour and compassion/esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous manner: voluntary adoption of a reversed judgement frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour (in the good sense) is the talent of being able voluntarily to put oneself into a mental disposition in which everything is judged quite differently from the ordinary method (reversed), yet in accordance with rational principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humorous manner belongs more to 'pleasant' than 'beautiful' art because beautiful art needs intrinsic worth and a certain seriousness. One who is involuntarily subject to such moods is 'a man of humours', whereas the skillful assumptor is 'humorous' and may use contrast to excite laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antinomy of taste: judgements both non-conceptual and universal
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an apparent antinomy: (Thesis) the judgement of taste is not based upon concepts (otherwise it would admit of controversy); (Antithesis) the judgement of taste is based on concepts (otherwise we could not quarrel about it and claim universal assent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant's solution: the judgement of taste refers to a concept in two different senses — not to determinate concepts (so it cannot be proved) but to an indeterminate, supersensible concept that grounds its claimed universality. Thus taste cannot be given a definite objective rule derivable by proof, yet it can claim validity for everyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas and genius: aesthetical (inexponible) vs rational (indemonstrable) Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas are representations that can never become cognition; aesthetical Ideas are intuitions of the Imagination (inexponible), rational Ideas are transcendent concepts of Reason (indemonstrable); genius is the faculty of aesthetical Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because aesthetical Ideas cannot be expounded into determinate concepts, genius (as the faculty producing them) supplies the subjective standard for art where rule or precept cannot. This explains why artistic production by genius follows nature rather than premeditated purpose.
